title: Church Machine IDE
description: A guided first run from source to protected execution.
speakerNotes: HOOK: What if the same browser window could be your editor, simulator, debugger, and hardware console? Today we will use one small program to connect all four.\nTiming: 1:00. Cue: welcome the room; ask who has used an IDE before. Outcome: audience understands this is a working environment, not a passive reference page. Fallback: use the workflow ribbon on the slide as the visual opening. Source: simulator/index.html title and meta description.

title: One IDE, five jobs
description: The browser is the control room for the whole learning loop.
speakerNotes: HOOK: Beginners do not need five tools before they can write one program—the IDE keeps the loop in one place.\nTiming: 2:00. Cue: trace the five cards left to right. Outcome: name simulator, assembler/compiler, Namespace explorer, debugging views, and FPGA test interface. Fallback: point to the cards without navigating live. Source: simulator/index.html; docs/StartupCM.md.

title: Your first five minutes
speakerNotes: HOOK: The fastest way to learn the IDE is not to memorize the ISA; it is to watch one tiny result travel through the interface.\nTiming: 2:00. Cue: ask audience to predict the result before revealing it. Outcome: a repeatable first-run recipe. Fallback: use the five-step diagram as a dry run. Source: simulator/index.html controls and tutorial views.

title: Small example: 2 + 3
description: A tiny program makes the interface legible.
speakerNotes: HOOK: Five lines are enough to make the machine visible. We will not hide the learning under a large application.\nTiming: 3:00. Cue: live demo—open Programs / Editor, choose Assembly, enter the shown program, click Assemble & Run. Expected: output shows 5; the console/listing updates. Fallback: show the static editor mock and narrate the expected output. Source: simulator/index.html; simulator/app-run.js.

title: Read the result, then the trace
description: Output says what happened; trace shows how it happened.
speakerNotes: HOOK: A correct answer is useful; a visible path to that answer is how you learn.\nTiming: 2:30. Cue: live demo—open output/trace and point to the current instruction, register changes, and next instruction. Expected: audience can distinguish program output from execution evidence. Fallback: use the trace lane on the slide. Source: simulator/app-memory.js and simulator UI trace/fault views.

title: Choose your entry point
description: Start concrete, then move up the vocabulary ladder.
speakerNotes: HOOK: The IDE lets you begin where your thinking is today: machine-shaped Assembly or named, higher-level forms.\nTiming: 2:00. Cue: show Code menu and tutorial selector; emphasize that this is a choice of entry point, not a required detour. Outcome: audience knows where to find Assembly, CLOOMC++/pet-name examples, JavaScript, Haskell, and Lambda material as available in the current IDE. Fallback: keep the slide’s ladder and mark languages as entry points, not promises of identical syntax. Source: simulator/index.html language detection and tutorial menu.

title: Capabilities: authority travels with the handle
description: A capability is not just an address; it is permission to act.
speakerNotes: HOOK: The key question is not “where is the object?” but “what am I allowed to do with it?”\nTiming: 2:30. Cue: ask audience to read R/W/X/E aloud; reveal that the handle carries authority and the machine checks it at use. Outcome: capability is understood conceptually, without bit-field detail. Fallback: use the four permission chips as the explanation. Source: simulator/app-run.js rights display; docs/namespace-vocabulary-tutorial.md.

title: C-List + LUMP: vocabulary in a package
description: The program gets a bounded vocabulary; the LUMP packages the implementation.
speakerNotes: HOOK: A program should not know every word in the machine—only the words it has been given.\nTiming: 2:30. Cue: explain C-List as available capability entries and LUMP as packaged code/data plus metadata; defer binary layout. Outcome: audience can say what each term does. Fallback: use the two-column diagram. Source: simulator/app-run.js listing; simulator/app-lump-editor.js; docs/namespace-json.md.

title: Namespace: the machine’s named layout
description: From raw slots to a readable map of abstractions.
speakerNotes: HOOK: The Namespace is where names stop floating in documentation and become a machine layout you can inspect.\nTiming: 2:30. Cue: open Builder → Namespace or the Namespace tutorial; point out Bootstrap, Resident, Freespace, and NS Table as concepts, not a binary-layout lesson. Expected: audience knows where to inspect slots and labels. Fallback: use the simplified map; explicitly defer addresses and packed fields. Source: simulator/namespace_tutorial.js; docs/namespace-json.md.

title: When something goes wrong
description: Faults are signposts, not dead ends.
speakerNotes: HOOK: A fault is the machine telling you which promise was broken—permission, presence, or state—not merely “it crashed.”\nTiming: 2:00. Cue: show fault and trace views; pause on the fault line, then identify the relevant capability or slot. Expected: audience has a debugging order: read fault → locate instruction → inspect capability/Namespace context. Fallback: use the three-step debug loop. Source: simulator/index.html fault/debug controls; simulator/app-memory.js.

title: Find the next answer inside the IDE
description: Tutorials for the path; Reference for the details.
speakerNotes: HOOK: Good tools do not make you leave the moment you have a question—they show you where the next answer lives.\nTiming: 1:30. Cue: open Tutorial for guided steps, Reference for architecture pages, and the hamburger menu for the full directory. Outcome: audience can self-serve after the session. Fallback: leave the resource list visible. Source: simulator/index.html Tutorial and Reference menu entries.

title: FPGA: baked-in boot, live bridge
description: Two phases, two responsibilities—do not mix them up.
speakerNotes: HOOK: The FPGA does not wait for the bridge to teach it how to boot; the bitstream already contains the approved startup state.\nTiming: 3:00. Cue: distinguish Phase A synthesis/bitstream from Phase B bridge observation/control. Explain that the bridge connects after boot for trace, step, run, halt, and breakpoints. Expected: no one leaves thinking the bridge performs boot loading. Fallback: use the handoff diagram and explicitly say “no live hardware promise.” Source: docs/StartupCM.md lines 10–24, 49–76, 186–225.

title: Hands-on: make the path yours
description: A 7-minute exercise to turn the tour into muscle memory.
speakerNotes: HOOK: You are ready when you can explain not only the answer, but which authority and which view made it possible.\nTiming: 4:00 plus 3:00 work time. Cue: ask pairs to run 2+3, change one operand, inspect output and trace, then find the Namespace entry involved. Expected: each pair can report result, one trace observation, and one place they would look after a fault. Fallback: use the static example and complete the questions verbally. Source: first-run workflow and current IDE navigation.

title: The path forward
description: Simulator first. Namespace next. Hardware when ready.
speakerNotes: HOOK: One small program gave us the whole map: enter, run, inspect, name authority, explore Namespace, then test the handoff.\nTiming: 1:30 plus Q&A. Cue: recap the four takeaways and invite questions. Next steps: repeat with a tutorial example; open Reference for deeper concepts; explore Builder/Namespace; use FPGA Connect/testing only with a prepared bitstream and bridge. Fallback: share the resource list on the slide. Source: simulator/index.html; docs/StartupCM.md; docs/namespace-vocabulary-tutorial.md.
